name: Mnasalcas
bio: Mnasalcas is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century BC (?). Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 9, 125, 128, 264, 268).

poems.title: Book VI, 9
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Here hang as gifts from Promachus to thee, Phoebus, his crooked bow and quiver that delights in arrows; but his winged shafts, the deadly gifts he sent his foes, are in the hearts of men on the field of battle.

poems.title: Book VI, 125
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Now I rest here far from the battle, I who often saved my lord’s fair breast by my back. Though receiving far-flying arrows and dreadful stones in thousands and long lances, I aver I never quitted Cleitus’ long arm in the horrid din of battle.

poems.title: Book VI, 128
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Rest in this holy house, bright shield, a gift from the wars to Artemis, Leto’s child. For oft in the battle, fighting on Alexander’s arm, thou didst in comely wise befoul with dust thy golden rim.

poems.title: Book VI, 264
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: I am the shield of Alexander, Phylleus’ son, and hang here a holy gift to golden-haired Apollo. My edge is old and war-worn, old and worn is my boss, but I shine by the valour I attained going forth to the battle with the bravest of men, him who dedicated me. From the day of my birth up I have remained unconquered,

poems.title: Book VI, 268
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: This image, Holy Artemis, Cleonymus set up to thee. Bestow thy blessing on this upland chase when thy feet, our lady, tread the forest-clad mountain, as thou followest eagerly the dreadful panting of thy pack.

poems.title: Book VII, 54: On the Same
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Ascra, the land of broad corn-fields, was my country, but the land of the charioteer Minyae holds my bones now I am dead. I am Hesiod, the most glorious in the eyes of the world of men who are judged by the test of wisdom.

poems.title: Book VII, 171
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Here, too, the birds of heaven shall rest their swift wings, alighting on this sweet plane-tree. For Poemander of Melos is dead, and cometh here no longer, his fowling canes smeared with lime.

poems.title: Book VII, 192: On a Locust
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: No longer, locust, sitting in the fruitful furrows shalt thou sing with thy shrill-toned wings, nor shalt thou delight me as I lie under the shade of the leaves, striking sweet music from thy tawny wings.

poems.title: Book VII, 194
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: This clay vessel set beside the far-reaching road holds the body of Democritus’ locust that made music with its wings. When it started to sing its long evening hymn, all the house rang with the melodious song.

poems.title: Book VII, 212: On a Mare
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Stranger, say that this is the tomb of wind-footed Aethyia, a child of the dry land, lightest of limb; often toiling over the long course, she, like a bird, travelled as far as do the ships.

poems.title: Book VII, 242
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: These men delivering their country from the tearful yoke that rested on her neck, clothed themselves in the dark dust. High praise win they by their valour, and let each citizen looking on them dare to die for his country.

poems.title: Book VII, 488
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Alas! Aristocrateia, thou art gone to deep Acheron, gone to rest before thy prime, before thy marriage; and naught but tears is left for thy mother, who reclining on thy tomb often bewails thee.

poems.title: Book VII, 491
poems.author: Mnasalcas
poems.text: Woe worth baleful virginity, for which, delightful Cleo, thou didst cut short thy bright youth! We stones in the semblance of Sirens stand on thy tomb tearing our cheeks for thee and weeping.
